content.title: About
content.content: Parmesan, dry grated, reduced fat (528) is a grated Parmesan cheese made from skimmed milk. It retains the characteristic nutty aroma and intense flavor of traditional Parmesan while containing less fat and fewer calories, making it a convenient ingredient for diet‑friendly cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Parmesan is one of the oldest cheeses in the world, produced in Italy for over 800 years.
Grated Parmesan is a universal seasoning – it is added to pasta, risotto, soups, and salads.
Reduced‑fat version is achieved by using skimmed milk and longer fermentation, preserving the crystalline protein structure.
Parmesan holds a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) status – only cheese produced in specific Italian regions may be called Parmesan.
Dry grated Parmesan stores well at room temperature, retaining its aroma for months.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Parmesan provides about 35 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich source of calcium
items.content: It is one of the most calcium‑dense cheeses, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Lower fat makes it more suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Probiotic properties
items.content: Fermentation creates beneficial bacteria that can support gut microbiota.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although lactose levels are low, individuals with severe intolerance may still experience symptoms.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Parmesan is salty; people monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to casein, the main milk protein.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dry grated Parmesan can be sprinkled over pasta, casseroles, vegetables, and soups. It can be added to sauces or used as a finishing garnish. For diet dishes, 1–2 tablespoons are enough to add flavor without excess calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep Parmesan in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, refrigerate to preserve aroma and prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Fufu is a traditional dish made from boiled and pounded starchy root vegetables (commonly cassava, yam or plantain), popular across West and Central Africa. It has a soft, slightly sticky texture and a neutral flavor, making it a versatile base for soups, stews and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fufu is traditionally prepared by hand, pounding the cooked root in a large wooden mortar.
There are many regional variations: Nigeria uses yam, Ghana prefers cassava, Cameroon often uses plantain.
It is typically served in small balls that are picked up with the fingers and dipped into sauce.
The dish is considered a symbol of hospitality and family tradition.
In some cultures fufu is called “the food of strength,” providing energy for hard labor.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Fufu provides slowly digestible carbs that give sustained energy and promote satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Traditional fufu contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: The root vegetables used in fufu supply fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Depending on the base ingredient, fufu can provide vitamin C, potassium and magnesium.

items.title: Hypoallergenic
items.content: For most people fufu does not trigger allergies, as it is free from nuts, gluten and dairy.

items.title: Cyanogenic compounds
items.content: Some varieties of raw cassava contain cyanogenic glycosides that can be toxic if not properly cooked.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Fufu can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, so individuals with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Potential contamination
items.content: Improper storage of the raw roots can lead to mold or bacterial growth, making the product unsafe.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fufu is usually served hot, shaped into small balls that are picked up with the fingers and dipped into meat, fish or vegetable sauces. It can also be used as a base for casseroles or added to soups as a thickener.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh roots (cassava, yam, plantain) in a cool, dry place or refrigerate for up to 3–5 days. Cooked fufu keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days; for longer storage freeze in portion‑size bags.

green-beans-canned-reduced-sodium-cooked.title: Green beans, canned, reduced sodium, cooked with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Canned green beans that are prepared with reduced sodium and cooked in vegetable oil provide a ready‑to‑eat vegetable side. The beans retain most of their nutrients, and the added oil enhances flavor and aids absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are a good source of fiber, B‑vitamins, and vitamin C.
Reduced‑sodium canning helps lower the risk of high blood pressure.
Cooking in oil preserves aroma and makes the beans more satisfying.
Canned beans have a long shelf life without refrigeration.
They are a convenient fresh‑vegetable alternative during winter months.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Lower salt content helps manage blood pressure.

items.title: Fat‑soluble vitamins from oil
items.content: The added oil aids absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Even reduced‑sodium products still contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor total intake.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beans.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands may use additives such as benzoates; check labels if you are sensitive.

items.title: Caloric contribution from oil
items.content: Oil adds calories, so portion size should be considered in calorie‑controlled diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Green beans can be eaten cold in salads, warmed in the microwave or skillet, added to soups, stews, and casseroles. They pair well with garlic, lemon, herbs, and lean proteins such as chicken or fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer beans to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 5‑7 days. Discard if an off‑odor or discoloration appears.

hot-dog-sandwich-beef-on-white-bread.title: Hot Dog Sandwich, Beef, on White Bread

content.title: About
content.content: A hot dog sandwich with beef is a sandwich that places a juicy beef sausage between two slices of soft white bread. It is often served with mustard, ketchup, pickles, and onions. The product is popular in fast‑food venues and as a quick snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional hot dogs are usually made with pork or beef sausage; the beef version is considered more "hearty" and is common in the United States.
White bread gives a soft texture but loses crunch quickly if the sandwich sits for a while.
The first hot dog is believed to have appeared in the late 19th century in New York, and the name derives from the German "dach" meaning sausage.
In the US more than 20 billion hot dogs are sold each year, a large share of which are beef‑based.
A typical beef hot dog contains about 150 kcal, while a slice of white bread adds roughly 80 kcal.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Beef sausage provides about 10 g of protein per serving, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of protein and carbohydrates makes the sandwich a quick source of energy.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The dense meat and bread together promote a feeling of fullness.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Beef sausages often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: A sausage may contain up to 8 g of saturated fat, which should be considered in low‑fat diets.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: White bread contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some pre‑made sausages contain nitrites and other preservatives that can be harmful in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hot dog hot, lightly toasting the bread until golden. Add mustard, ketchup, pickles, onions, or coleslaw to taste. It pairs well with french fries or a fresh salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked sausages refrigerated at ≤ 4 °C and use within 3‑4 days. Store bread in a dry place in a sealed bag to prevent drying. Sausages freeze well for up to 2 months; thaw in the refrigerator before use.

infant-formula-similac-for-spit-up-ready.title: Infant formula, Similac for Spit-Up, ready-to-feed

content.title: About
content.content: Infant formula, Similac for Spit-Up is a ready-to-feed baby milk substitute designed specifically for infants prone to spit‑up. The formula contains easily digestible proteins, probiotics, and a moderate amount of fat to help reduce post‑feeding discomfort.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Similac for Spit‑Up is formulated according to pediatric recommendations to reduce gas buildup.
The product comes in sterile, ready‑to‑use containers that require no preparation.
It includes prebiotics that support the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.
The formula contains DHA and ARA – essential fatty acids for brain and eye development.
Clinical studies have confirmed its effectiveness in lowering spit‑up incidents.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Proteins are partially hydrolyzed, making them easier for infants to digest.

items.title: Supports gut microbiome
items.content: Probiotics and prebiotics promote the growth of beneficial intestinal bacteria.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA aid normal development of the nervous system and vision.

items.title: Reduces gas
items.content: The composition helps lower gas production that can cause spit‑up and discomfort.

items.title: Balanced nutrition
items.content: The formula provides essential vitamins and minerals needed for growth.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Children with known cow‑milk allergy may react to this product.

items.title: Lactose content
items.content: Infants with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort.

items.title: Shelf life after opening
items.content: Once opened, the product should be used within 48 hours and kept refrigerated.

items.title: Temperature control
items.content: Do not serve the product too hot – check temperature before feeding.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve the ready‑to‑feed product directly after opening the container. If desired, cool to room temperature. Do not dilute or microwave, as this may affect probiotic integrity.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened containers in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 48 hours. Discard if the product develops an off‑smell, color, or taste.

content.title: About
content.content: A muffin is a small, individual portion of baked good made from whole grain white flour, often enriched with dried fruit, nuts, or spices. It has a soft, slightly moist crumb and the characteristic aroma of traditional English recipes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Muffins originated in England in the 19th century as a quick way to use leftover batter.
The whole‑grain version retains more fiber and nutrients than a classic white muffin.
In the United States muffins are commonly eaten for breakfast, while in the United Kingdom they are enjoyed at any time of day.
There are countless variations: blueberry, banana, carrot, nut, and even spiced versions with cinnamon or ginger.
Traditional English muffins are often split, toasted, and served with butter and jam.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole grain flour provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates deliver sustained energy and help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B2 and B3 vitamins aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: When berries or nuts are added, they contribute antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Using plant oils keeps saturated fat levels lower than many other baked goods.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole grain flour contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some recipes add a notable amount of sugar; those monitoring blood glucose should choose lower‑sugar versions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even whole grain muffins are calorie‑dense and can contribute to weight gain if eaten in excess.

items.title: Oil content
items.content: A generous amount of oil raises the fat content; moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins can be enjoyed as a snack on their own, split and spread with butter, cream cheese, or nut butter. They pair well with tea or coffee. For extra texture, toast them briefly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Warm before serving in an oven or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with peas is a whole‑grain rice cooked together with green peas. The rice retains its bran and germ, making it more nutritious, while peas add plant protein and a pleasant sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice contains more fiber and B‑vitamins than white rice.
Peas are one of the oldest cultivated legumes, grown for over 10,000 years.
The rice‑and‑pea combination is common in traditional Asian and Mediterranean dishes.
Brown rice has a lower glycemic index than white rice, helping to stabilize blood sugar.
Peas are rich in lysine, an amino acid often limited in cereals.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and maintains gut health.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Peas add about 5 g of protein per 100 g, making the dish a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are essential for muscle function, nerve signaling, and bone formation.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Brown rice raises blood glucose slowly, beneficial for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Rice bran provides phenolic compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid in whole grains can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: High carbohydrate load
items.content: For those on strict low‑carb diets, the portion size may be too calorie‑dense.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brown rice with peas can be served as a side dish with meat, fish, or vegetables, added to salads, soups, or casseroles. Rinse the rice before cooking and soak the peas for 2–3 hours for even cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, refrigerate to prevent oxidation of the bran oils.
